title: Dhruva opens his eyes
hookLine: Dhruva holds Vishnu in his heart, then opens his eyes to find him there; darshan
carry: darshan is seeing god, and being seen
last: A MANDIR IS GOD'S HOUSE; WE COME AS GUESTS.

cards: A five-year-old prince named Dhruva tries to climb onto his father's lap. His stepmother pulls him away: you're not my son, so you don't belong there. If you want a place like that, go and pray to Vishnu.
So he does. He walks into the forest and, taught by a sage, sits and holds Vishnu's form in his heart, month after month, until even the gods feel the weight of his prayer.
Then one day, the form he's been seeing inside suddenly disappears. Startled, Dhruva opens his eyes.

teach.h: DHRUVA OPENS HIS EYES: VISHNU IS THERE.
teach.b: And there in front of him stands Vishnu: the same form he'd held inside, now outside, looking back at him.
The boy is so overcome he can't speak, until Vishnu touches his cheek with his conch shell and praise pours out of him.
That's the Bhagavata Purana, and Dhruva, it says, was given the pole star, the one star that doesn't move. That moment has a name, and it's the teaching today: darshan.
It comes from the Sanskrit root drish, to see. In a temple it means to stand before God and look, and to be looked at in return. That second half is the surprise.
Many Hindus understand the murti as truly inhabited, so the seeing goes both ways.

teach.h: THE EYES ARE OPENED IN THE RITE.
teach.b: That's why the eyes of the image matter so much: often large and bright, sometimes silver. In the rites that install a new image, there is a moment for opening its eyes, and after that, the image is said to see.
In some temples a curtain covers the shrine at times, and when it opens, the crowd leans forward: darshan! Hands come together. Some say a name under their breath.
Some just look. You can take darshan of a holy person, a sacred river, a mountain. And the classical schools of Hindu philosophy are called darshanas, ways of seeing.
So that's why people wait six hours in line for three seconds at the front. They aren't only looking at God.

teach.h: DARSHAN IS SEEING GOD, AND BEING SEEN.
teach.b: Like Dhruva, they're being seen. Three seconds can be enough, if you actually look.

how: Hindus go to temples for darshan, standing before the murti with folded hands to see the deity and be seen in return; many also speak of taking darshan of saints, sacred rivers and holy places.

o: a silent prayer said in front of a statue
a long pilgrimage on foot to a shrine
seeing the divine, and being seen in return

p: opened his eyes to find Vishnu there
to see God and be seen

s: darshan only means looking at a statue
many Hindus understand the seeing goes both ways: the devotee is seen too.
Dhruva was given the pole star
in the Bhagavata Purana, the boy who saw Vishnu gets the star that doesn't move.
you can take darshan of a holy person or a sacred river
wherever the holy is present, you can go to see it and be seen.

games.q: you've waited hours in line at a well-known temple. you get three seconds in front of the image. what do you do with them?
o: look, with folded hands, and let yourself be seen.
use them to recite a long list of requests.
games.why: darshan is seeing and being seen. many people just look, hands together, maybe saying a name under their breath.

practice: Let your gaze rest softly on an image that matters to you, the murti in your corner, a picture of a deity, a photo of a teacher or someone you love, or simply the sky out the window, especially on the eyes if there are eyes.
Don't analyze it; just look, the way you'd look at someone you've missed. Then turn it around and stay with both: what would it be like to be seen like this, fully, without judgment?

wordCard.voice: Darshan. Seeing: standing before God, a holy person or a holy place, to see and to be seen in return. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit darśana: seeing, a sight, a vision; also a school of philosophy.

carryVoice: Your line: darshan is seeing God, and being seen. Dhruva opened his eyes, and Vishnu was looking back. Day one hundred thirty-three.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 4.8–9 (Dhruva's austerity; Vishnu appears as the inner vision vanishes; the conch touches his cheek; the pole star)
